title: Sorting firms: sector, ownership and size

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Sort a firm by sector of production, by ownership and by size, and place a firm whose activities span several sectors.

blocks.heading: Three ways to sort a firm
blocks.text: A firm is a business that makes or sells goods or services, and economics sorts firms in three ways. By sector of production: primary firms extract or grow raw materials, such as a fishing firm at Walvis Bay; secondary firms process those materials into goods, such as a canning plant; tertiary firms supply services, such as the transport that moves the cans to shops. By ownership: a private-sector firm belongs to private individuals or groups who take the risk in the hope of profit, whereas a public-sector firm, also called a state-owned firm, belongs to the government, which appoints who runs it. By size: few workers and a small output make a firm small; many workers and a large output make it large.

blocks.heading: One firm, three sectors
blocks.text: Otjiwa Dairy in Gobabis works in all three sectors at once. Its own herd of 300 cows gives N$1.2 million of raw milk a year - farming is primary activity. Its pasteurising plant turns the milk into 400 000 tubs of yoghurt - processing is secondary activity. Its 6 vans deliver the tubs to shops across the region - a delivery service is tertiary activity. Classifying such a firm means sorting its activities one by one. A Japanese firm that catches its own fish, cans them and sells them through its own stalls makes the same point: a firm is not stuck in one sector by its name.

blocks.heading: Wanting a price rise is not what causes one
blocks.text: Learners mix up two different statements: the reason any firm prefers to charge more, and the reason a merger can leave buyers paying more. The boundary: wanting a higher price is a motive firms generally share - a higher price usually means more revenue from each sale - and it exists whether or not any merger happens. A merger resulting in higher prices is an outcome, which may follow where the joining removes one of the market's competing sellers, so the pressure of rivalry on price weakens. The test: ask whether a statement names what a firm aims at, or what changed in the market - the same want existed before the merger, when prices did not rise, so it cannot explain what changed.
